rv.q: Danya Taymor presides over a perfect production that left me with my heart in my mouth and my pen scrambling across the page.
Will Arbery’s Heroes of the Fourth Turning is so frighteningly well written, it’s hard to write about.
Isabella Byrd offers a masterpiece of lighting design, rich with portent and glinting significance.
The astonishing new play explores the lives and ideas of conservatives with affection, understanding and deep knowledge — if not, ultimately, approval.
Heroes of the Fourth Turning is a tough watch, but it is absolutely necessary as America's competing tribes retreat into fortresses of affirmation.

A thoughtful, subtly satiric look at educated individuals of faith who desire to return America to the fundamental values of yesteryear, Heroes of the Fourth Turning may well annoy and even infuriate some viewers.
That the playwright makes this garrulous, opinionated crew so engaging -- and their concerns so relevant -- is a mark of his considerable imagination and empathy.
Terrifically acted and intellectually stimulating, “Heroes” is also eerie, at times confusing, too long and too dark.
It's a realistic choice, but one that diminishes the connection between the audience and the characters.
But Arbery hasn't connected the dramatic dots between the puking scene, nutty Justin and the noise-belching house.
Playwright Will Arbery admirably endeavors to craft a nuanced portrait of conservative Catholicism, but the result is a facile exploration of religious and political tribalism.
It’s all powerful and ugly, joyfully harsh and dynamic, giving words to those generally ignored in the New York theater world, with little to balance our liberal beliefs on.

Under Danya Taymor’s intuitive and exacting direction, the accomplished cast delivers believable and authentic performances and embodies the characteristics of Yeats’ rough beast with cathartic effect.
This thought-provoking piece should come with a glossary or, more to the point, a required reading list before attending.

Apart from how, in such darkness anyone could down a deer, this ritualistic prologue, soon followed by the main action, introduces us to an unusual, disturbing, rhetorically dense, only fitfully engaging drama.

cn.t: Critics mostly praise Arbery's nuanced, "frighteningly well written" portrait of Catholic conservatives, calling it brave and revelatory for depicting perspectives rarely seen on New York stages, though some find the exploration facile or messy.
